chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from an-Nadr ibn Suwayd from Muhammad ibn Abi Hamzah from Abu Khalid al-Qammam said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'Is the divorce of a foolish man who has lost his mind valid through his guardian?' He said, 'And why should he not divorce her himself?' I said: 'It is not certain that if he divorces her, he will not say tomorrow,
Or he may not know how to divorce properly.' He said, 'I see his guardian to be in the position of the ruler.'
And the divorce of a young child is valid if he understands the divorce, and the limit of that is ten years. What indicates this is what he narrated:

key_terms.اَلذَّاهِبُ اَلْعَقْلِ: One who has lost his mind/reason
key_terms.اَلسُّلْطَانُ: The ruler/authority (used here to denote the high status/authority of the guardian)
key_terms.اَلْأَحْمَقُ: The foolish man (a specific legal category of insanity/mental deficiency less severe than full insanity)
key_terms.عَشْرُ سِنِينَ: Ten years (the age limit for understanding divorce)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on the divorce of a mentally incompetent or foolish man in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi records this narration to clarify the legal status of the 'ahmaq' (person of limited intellect) in marital contracts, establishing that their guardian acts with the authority of a sovereign (sulṭān) to ensure validity. The Imam’s rhetorical question highlights the practical risk of self-denial by the individual, justifying the guardian's proxy role. Furthermore, it sets the threshold of 'bulugh al-ahliyyah' for divorce at ten years, linking physical maturity with the cognitive capacity to understand the act of separation.
